title: A Modulo That Is Never Negative
statement:
C++'s `%` truncates the same way `/` does, which means it can hand back a
**negative** result for a negative dividend: `-7 % 3` is `-1` in C++, not
the `2` a mathematician (or a candidate expecting Python's `%`) would
expect. Fixing that up looks like a one-line adjustment -- until the exact
same pair of values that makes plain division crash turns out to poison
the fix-up too.

## Your function

```
int TrueMod(int a, int b);
```

`b` is never `0`. Return the value `r` such that `0 <= r < |b|` and
`a - r` is evenly divisible by `b` -- the "always non-negative" remainder,
regardless of `a`'s or `b`'s own sign.

## Watch out

- **A negative result from `a % b` needs `|b|` added back, not `b`
  itself.** `%`'s result already has magnitude less than `|b|`, so one
  addition of `|b|` is always enough to land it in `[0, |b|)` -- the sign
  of `b` is irrelevant to how much to add, only to whether adding is
  needed at all (it is needed exactly when the raw result came back
  negative).
- **`a == INT_MIN` and `b == -1` is the one input where computing `a % b`
  at all is already too late.** The C++ standard defines `%` in terms of
  `/`, and `INT_MIN / -1` does not fit in a 32-bit `int` -- the same
  overflow that makes plain division crash on this pair makes `%` crash
  on it too, on real hardware, not just in principle. The only way to
  compute `TrueMod(INT_MIN, -1)` safely is to never evaluate `a % b` for
  it: recognise `b == -1` up front and return `0` directly, since
  everything is evenly divisible by `1` (or `-1`) and the true remainder
  is always `0` regardless of `a`.
- **Every other combination of `a` and `b` is completely ordinary.**
  `INT_MIN % 2`, for instance, is perfectly well-defined C++ (`INT_MIN` is
  even) -- the crash is specific to a divisor of exactly `-1`, not to
  `INT_MIN` on its own.

tests.name: positive a, positive b -- already non-negative
negative a, positive b -- C++'s raw % would be negative
